ru: В тылу́ рабо́тали же́нщины и де́ти.
en: Women and children worked on the home front.
en_alt: Women and children worked in the rear.
note: English says "on the home front", not "at"; the literal military reading is added as an alternative.

en_alt: Complete darkness was all around.
note: Equally valid word order for the word-bank drill.

en_alt: I gave my mum a red tulip.
note: ма́ме is glossed "mum", so accept that rendering too.

ru: Она́ не могла́ подня́ть таку́ю тя́жесть.
en: She could not lift such a weight.
en_alt: She could not lift such a heavy weight.
note: The Russian has no word for "heavy"; "such a weight" already carries it in English.

en_alt: They accused him of murder.
note: The Russian is an active impersonal plural; both renderings are standard.

en_alt: The police are searching for the killer.
note: и́щет is glossed "to search", so accept that verb too.

en_alt: The killer vanished into the darkness.
note: Equally natural rendering of скры́лся.

ru: Он отно́сится к лю́дям с уваже́нием.

en_alt: The teacher earned the pupils' respect.
note: Possessive word order is equally valid.

en_alt: There was an increase in prices.
note: More idiomatic English for произошло́; the existing rendering stays.
Всё (neuter singular "everything") cannot govern the 3rd-person-plural ждут; the intended word is Все "everyone".

en_alt: The shop is round the corner.
note: British English also says "round the corner".

en_alt: The table stands in the corner of the room.
note: стои́т renders equally well as "stands".
The English is right — you draw with charcoal — but the headword gloss "coal" does not cover that sense.

en_alt: The city lives under the threat of flooding.
note: го́род is glossed "city", so accept that too.

ru: Поли́ция не реаги́рует на пусты́е угро́зы.

en_alt: The vase broke from the blow.
note: разби́лась is equally "broke"; both are natural.

ru: Он получи́л си́льный уда́р по голове́.

note: «по́льзоваться уда́чей» is not idiomatic Russian (по́льзоваться успе́хом / ему́ везёт в дела́х), and "He enjoys luck in his affairs" is awkward English in the same way.

en_alt: We hope for luck.
note: Simple present is an equally valid rendering of the Russian present.

en_alt: Such luck is rare.
note: Natural alternative to "happens rarely".

en_alt: The children watched with surprise.
The children looked with surprise.
note: "looked on" adds a spectating nuance the Russian смотре́ли does not; the plainer renderings are accepted too.

ru: Пойдёшь с на́ми в кино́? — С удово́льствием!
en_alt: Are you coming to the cinema with us? — With pleasure!
note: The idiomatic "I'd love to!" is right for С удово́льствием!, but the literal reading teaches the phrase.

en_alt: The journey gave us a lot of pleasure.
note: Путеше́ствие is glossed "journey" and мно́го "a lot".

en_alt: I will help you with pleasure.
I will gladly help you.
note: Adds the literal с удово́льствием reading alongside the idiomatic "gladly".

ru: Я чита́ю э́ту кни́гу с удово́льствием.

en_alt: It is impossible to forget the horrors of war.
note: Literal rendering of невозмо́жно забы́ть, alongside the passive.

en_alt: He froze in horror.
note: "in horror" is at least as natural as "with horror" here.

ru: Она́ смотре́ла на э́то с у́жасом.
Я не могу́ развяза́ть э́тот у́зел.

note: A rope is not «соста́влена из» knots — a native speaker would say «На верёвке не́сколько узло́в» or «Верёвка завя́зана не́сколькими узла́ми»; the English faithfully reproduces the oddity.

en_alt: He tied a firm knot.
note: кре́пкий is glossed "strong"; "firm" tracks it more closely than "tight".

en_alt: Grandmother embroidered a napkin with patterns.
note: салфе́тка is specifically a napkin/doily; "cloth" is looser.

en_alt: We work on the boss's instructions.
note: Idiomatic English uses the plural "on instructions"; both are accepted.

en: He talked a lot about Ukraine.
en_alt: He said a lot about Ukraine.
note: "He told a lot about Ukraine" is not English — "tell" needs an object; "talked" carries расска́зывал.

en_alt: Ukraine is located in eastern Europe.
note: нахо́дится is glossed "to be located"; both renderings are natural.

en_alt: I met a Ukrainian.
note: познако́мился is the moment of meeting, so "I met" is equally valid.

en: The Ukrainian talked about his city.
en_alt: The Ukrainian told us about his city.
note: The Russian has no «нам» — "us" is added; the old rendering is kept as an alternative.

en_alt: She bought a golden ornament.
note: Equally valid rendering of золото́е.

en_alt: There is a stone in this ornament.
note: A stone set in jewellery is "in" it in English; both are accepted.

ru: По у́зким у́лицам ста́рого го́рода прия́тно гуля́ть ве́чером.
en_alt: It is pleasant to stroll along the narrow streets of the old city in the evening.
note: го́рода is glossed "city", so accept that rendering too.

ru: На у́лицах по́сле пра́здника остаётся мно́го му́сора.

en_alt: Children play in the streets of the city.
note: го́рода is glossed "city"; both are valid.

en_alt: It is raining outside.
note: На у́лице in a weather sentence idiomatically means "outside"; the literal en_gb stays for the улица drill.

en_alt: We went outside.
note: Common idiomatic reading of вы́шли на у́лицу.

en_alt: He is a man of great intelligence.
note: Equally natural rendering of большо́го ума́.

en_alt: Solve this problem in your mind.
note: Accepts the gloss-tracking "mind" alongside the idiomatic "head".

ru: В лу́чших университе́тах о́чень высо́кий ко́нкурс.
en_alt: At the best universities the competition is very high.
note: "for places" is implied rather than stated; the plainer version is accepted too.

ru: Он зна́ет язы́к на высо́ком у́ровне.

en_alt: We moved to a new level.
note: Equally valid rendering of перешли́ на.

en_alt: The peasants are harvesting.
The peasants gather the harvest.
note: Common English renderings of собира́ть урожа́й.

ru: На пе́рвых уро́ках но́вые ученики́ обы́чно молча́т.
en_alt: In the first lessons the new pupils are usually silent.
note: молча́т is glossed "to be silent"; both are natural.

en_alt: The Russian lesson begins at nine.
note: начина́ется is glossed "to begin".
A cat's усы́ are whiskers, so the English is right, but the headword gloss "moustache" does not cover that sense.

en_alt: He stroked one half of his moustache.
note: оди́н ус is one half of the moustache; both renderings work.

en: Thanks to joint efforts we won.
en_alt: Thanks to common efforts we won.
note: «о́бщими уси́лиями» is "joint efforts" in English; "common efforts" reads as translationese.

en_alt: He did me a big favour.
note: услу́га in this frame is idiomatically a "favour"; the literal en_gb stays.

en_alt: She is achieving success.
note: добива́ется is glossed "achieves"; the imperfective supports both readings.

en_alt: He struggles with tiredness.
note: бо́рется с is glossed "to struggle with"; both are natural.

en_alt: She fell asleep at once from tiredness.
note: More natural English word order; the existing rendering stays.

en_alt: After work he feels tiredness.
note: "feels tiredness" is not idiomatic English; the noun rendering is kept as an alternative for the word-bank drill.

en_alt: The installation started in the morning.
note: Equally valid rendering of начала́сь.

en_alt: The price of installing the air conditioner is high.
note: Gerund rendering of устано́вки is equally natural.
Here устро́йство means the make-up/workings of the car, a sense the headword gloss "device" does not cover; the English is right.

ru: Я не согла́сен с его́ утвержде́нием.
en_alt: I do not agree with his statement.
note: More literal rendering of не согла́сен; both are natural.

en_alt: He waited until morning at home.
He waited for morning at home.
note: дожда́лся у́тра is "waited until morning"; both readings are accepted.

ru: По утра́м он пьёт ко́фе и чита́ет но́вости.

note: ухо́д here means departure, which the headword gloss "care" does not cover; the English is right.

ru: Без ва́шего уча́стия мы не спра́вимся.

en_alt: They gave each participant a medal.
note: The Russian is an active impersonal plural; both renderings are standard.

en_alt: The participants of the competition prepared.
note: Equally valid word order.

en_alt: They bought a plot out of town.
note: за́ городом is idiomatically "out of town"; both are natural.
уча́сток here is a stretch/section of road, a sense the headword gloss "plot" does not cover; the English is right.
